system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- Evidence text comes from a PDF text layer. If symbols are garbled so that you cannot verify the atom, answer "hold" for that check and say so.
- Be strict. When unsure between pass and a non-pass value, choose the non-pass value and explain.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom. pass = fully stated. revise = the core claim is stated, and the gap is only wording, strength, or a dropped/extra peripheral qualifier that can be fixed by deleting or softening words (say what). fail = not stated, OR the atom adds substantive content the evidence lacks: a scope or population restriction (e.g. 'In B-ALL'), a mechanism or operation, a characterization (e.g. 'an unbounded while loop'), or a formula/definition. If deleting the unsupported part would change what the atom tests, it is fail, not revise. For pass, put the supporting evidence ids in cite (required).
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / revise / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge: one fact a person who studied the concept would simply know. revise = the core fact is recall-level but the sentence carries extra load that must be removed, e.g. stacked conditions (since/although/if ... and ...), a procedural or evaluative add-on ('easy to define but requires checking ...'), or a clause that introduces a second technical concept that must be known separately (e.g. 'if X is an inner Kan complex' when that is not the card concept). fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = the authors' opinion or choice, or the finding of one study, so the answer is not fixed without the source.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a single system, product, or one study's topic.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Disaggregating household aggregate consumption into appliance-level information, framed as classification and regression. Covers dataset sampling-rate groups, missing data and generalization to unseen houses, and HMM versus unsupervised/semi-supervised/supervised approaches; excludes the other energy services.

ATOMS:
- KGBDP-C09-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM), proposed by Hart, aims to give users appliance-level consumption information in a harmless way by disaggregating the aggregate consumption of an entire household, rather than installing meters throughout the household as Intrusive Load Monitoring would require.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0171-s10] Therefore, instead of the Intrusive Load Monitoring solution which influences users’ convenience, Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring was proposed by Hart in [183] with the main goal of providing users with the same information in a harmless way by aggregating entire household consumption at the appliance level, which can be seen in Fig. 1.
- KGBDP-C09-S1-02.r1a | S1
  ATOM: In Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring, classification is one of the two main problems and provides information about the activation of an appliance at the appliance level.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0171-s12] Having in mind the previous information, two main problems are present within the NILM literature - classification, which provides information about the activation on the appliance level, and regression for the estimation of the appliance’s individual consumption, as shown in the example Fig. 2.
- KGBDP-C09-S1-02.r1b | S1
  ATOM: In Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring, regression is one of the two main problems and estimates an appliance's individual consumption.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0171-s12] Having in mind the previous information, two main problems are present within the NILM literature - classification, which provides information about the activation on the appliance level, and regression for the estimation of the appliance’s individual consumption, as shown in the example Fig. 2.
- KGBDP-C09-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: NILM was motivated by a cited conclusion that up to 12% of residential energy consumption can be decreased by giving users feedback on how energy has been used, that is, which appliances use how much electrical energy.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0171-s07] NILM was motivated by conclusions, such as those from [70], which claimed that up to 12% of residential energy consumption can be decreased by giving users feedback on how the energy has been used.
    [KGBDP-p0171-s08] In other words, by providing the user with information about which of their appliances is using electrical energy and how much, significant savings can be reached.
- KGBDP-C09-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: Hidden Markov Models suit NILM because they model processes with unobservable states, so individual appliance consumption can be estimated from the observable output, the aggregated consumption.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0174-s07] They were designed to model the processes with unobservable states, which is indeed the case with the NILM problem.
    [KGBDP-p0174-s08] In other words, the goal is to estimate individual consumption in accordance with the observable output (aggregated consumption).
- KGBDP-C09-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Supervised NILM approaches are widely used, with neural networks the largest group, chiefly Recurrent Neural Networks (especially LSTM) and Convolutional Neural Networks (including Denoising Autoencoders), whose ability to extract complex features from input sequences was confirmed to increase prediction performance.

- KGBDP-C09-S2-03.r1 | S2
  ATOM: Many NILM authors use unsupervised learning techniques instead of improving generalization of supervised ones, because labeled data are not available for the houses in which services are going to be installed.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0174-s13] The main cause of this is the fact that labeled data for the houses in which services are going to be installed are not available, as already discussed.
    [KGBDP-p0174-s14] Therefore, many authors choose to use unsupervised learning techniques instead of improving generalization on the supervised ones.

    [KGBDP-p0173-s16] Bearing all of this in mind, validating the results from the data coming from the house whose measurements have already been used in the training process is considered inadequate.
    [KGBDP-p0173-s17] Thus, it is accepted that for validation and testing purposes one, so called, unseen house is set aside and
- KGBDP-C09-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Generalization is even more crucial for NILM than in many other machine learning fields, because different houses may contain different types of the same appliance, so performance on a house not used in training may be significantly lower than the estimated one.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0173-s13] Even though the problem of achieving as high performance as possible on the testing rather than training domain is a hot topic in many fields of research within Machine Learning (ML) and Big Data, the generalization problem is even more crucial for NILM.

  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0173-s09] For example, in the case of refrigerators, this is a minor problem which can be neglected because it works circularly, so each approximately 20 min it turns on or off, leading to numerous examples of both active and inactive working periods.
    [KGBDP-p0173-s10] By contrast, when, for example, a washing machine is considered, dropping down the sequence of its activation is unacceptable as it is turned on twice a week in a household on average, so it is difficult to collect enough data for training purposes.
